question: Yet another year of serious teacher shortages is affecting pupils’ educational rights. In Greece, thousands of schools are starting the year without the teachers they need. This is especially true in the area of special needs, where the shortfall is enormous. Every year, schools take on more than 40 000 supply teachers, while 4 000 to 7 000 teachers retire.

The number of teachers recruited on permanent contracts is insufficient. Following a policy of spending cuts – while simultaneously pouring EUR 26 billion into the arms industry – the Nea Dimokratia Government has decided against hiring the necessary staff, instead choosing to spread resources more thinly, resulting in classrooms of more than 30 children.

The policy of hiring minimal permanent staff and expanding flexible working arrangements has left tens of thousands of supply teachers in a precarious situation. Teachers’ salaries remain low, while the high cost of living and the lack of affordable housing make it impossible to get by. In the light of the above, what view does the Commission take of: 1.
the fact that the enormous teacher shortages and delays in filling vacancies result in thousands of children being deprived of the right to education?

the fact that the EU’s policy of ‘budget cuts’ and ‘spending rationalisation’ is driven by the arms race of the war economy and leads to fewer permanent appointments, the widespread use of flexible work contracts and the shifting of education-related costs onto working-class families?
the fact that, as denounced by teacher associations in Greece and across the EU, such large class sizes make a meaningful and efficient educational process impossible?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (6.11.2025) The Commission is aware that teacher shortages have become a major concern across the EU, placing additional strain on the existing workforce. Shortages are closely connected to the broader challenge of the low attractiveness of the teaching profession.

The Union of Skills1 announced an EU Teachers and Trainers Agenda in 2026, to help Member States tackle teacher shortages, improving teachers’ working conditions, and improving career prospects. Also, approximately 1 billion EUR is foreseen under European Social Fund Plus to support the education and training systems in Greece.

The Commission recalls that Directive 1999/702 requires Member States to adopt effective measures to prevent abuse of successive fixed-term employment contracts but leaves Member States a certain margin of discretion as to how they achieve this objective. The Treaties do not confer to the EU competence to adopt binding guidelines on how to prevent abuse of such contracts in the Greek school system.

Since 2019, following a decade of no hirings in education, Greece proceeded with permanent appointments of teachers to address staff shortages in schools and phase out the extensive use of substitute teachers. However, existing public data does not allow to assess whether all needs are covered. A reduction of school students is projected for the coming years.
Reliable data as well as systematic monitoring of the teaching force would be necessary to understand the changing demand for qualified teachers.
1 COM(2025) 90 final. 2 Council Directive 1999/70/EC of 28 June 1999 concerning the framework agreement on fixed-term work
concluded by ETUC, UNICE and CEEP (OJ L 175, 10.7.1999, p. 43) - https://eurlex.europa.eu/eli/dir/1999/70/oj/eng.
